science-of-immunity.title: The science of immunity: which vitamins really matter for kids
science-of-immunity.excerpt: Not all immunity products are equal. Here is what research says about building strong defences in children.
science-of-immunity.body:
A child's immune system keeps developing into adolescence, and during that period it is especially sensitive to micronutrient gaps. Vitamin D3, vitamin C and zinc have the strongest evidence base.

Vitamin D3 is involved in the work of innate immune cells. In regions with little sunlight most children are deficient, so supplementation in autumn and winter is justified.

Vitamin C does not prevent a cold, but it shortens its duration. Regular intake works better than large doses taken once symptoms appear.

Probiotics affect immunity indirectly: about 70 % of immune cells live in the gut, so healthy microflora is part of the body's defence.

gut-is-the-second-brain.title: Why gut health matters for a child's growth
gut-is-the-second-brain.excerpt: Gut microflora affects not only digestion, but also immunity, mood and overall wellbeing.
gut-is-the-second-brain.body:
The gut–brain axis is one of the most fascinating areas of modern science. Understanding it can change the way you approach your child's health.

Microflora takes part in synthesising B vitamins and vitamin K and helps absorb calcium and iron — exactly the elements that matter most during rapid growth.

Diet changes, travel and antibiotic courses disturb the bacterial balance. In such periods probiotics help restore microflora faster.

Signs worth paying attention to: irregular stool, bloating, reduced appetite and frequent colds.

focus-and-brain-development.title: How to support your child's focus and brain development
focus-and-brain-development.excerpt: Which nutrients help children concentrate, learn and remember new information better.
focus-and-brain-development.body:
A child's brain is roughly 60 % fat, and a significant share of it is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) from the omega-3 group.

DHA is part of neuronal cell membranes and affects how fast signals travel. Studies link sufficient omega-3 levels with better attention and school performance.

Iron and iodine are responsible for cognitive development, while B vitamins support energy metabolism in nervous tissue.

One important note: supplements only work alongside proper sleep, physical activity and a varied diet.

healthy-snacks-for-active-kids.title: Healthy snacks for active kids
healthy-snacks-for-active-kids.excerpt: Which foods and habits help a child get more energy and the vitamins they need every day.
healthy-snacks-for-active-kids.body:
A snack is not “extra food” — it is a full part of a child's diet, providing up to a quarter of daily energy.

A good snack combines slow carbohydrates, protein and a little fat: wholegrain bread with cheese, yoghurt with berries or a handful of nuts with fruit.

Sweet bars and juices give a quick energy spike followed by an equally quick crash — an hour later the child is hungry and distracted again.

Vitamin complexes complement the diet but do not replace it. The gummy format helps make intake a daily habit without negotiation.
